subtype: Approach: resource and budget planning [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday, 11 p.m.
Planning meeting in Madhav's room today for Manali in December. Everyone was shouting place names, so I took the notebook and made them stop. First question: what will it actually cost?
Bus both ways for the five of us: 12,000. Homestay, three nights: 9,000. Food: 7,500 if we're not silly. Entry fees, the cable car and local cabs: 3,500. Total 32,000.
Then I thought, every trip goes over. Last year's Rishikesh trip did, and Madhav had to borrow from his cousin. So I added ten percent, 3,200, for surprises. 35,200.
Divided by five: 7,040 each. Madhav went quiet, then said, 'That's doable if I start now.' We have ten weeks, so roughly 700 a week each.
Feels good to have a real number instead of vibes 🙂
– Ganga

qa.a: Total 32,000.

Since you're in charge of tickets, here's how I worked out our dates. Tell me if I've missed something.
My last exam is on 19 December. Yours and Meenu's end on the 20th. College reopens on 2 January, and Arif has his cousin's wedding on the 29th. So the only clean window is 21 to 28 December.
Now, everything depends on the train to Kochi. It's a 36-hour journey and the holiday trains fill up fast. If we leave on the evening of the 21st, we reach on the morning of the 23rd, and a train back on the night of the 26th gets us home on the 28th, a day before the wedding.
So please book trains first, today if you can. The homestay in Fort Kochi can wait a few days. There are plenty, and we can match them to whatever train dates we get.
Farida

Madhuri, you asked how our group of six managed Hampi in the middle of semester. This is Kiran, official calendar nerd, so here's the secret: we started from the end, not the beginning.
First I wrote down every hard date. Internal exams till 11 October. Two of us had a lab viva on the 16th. Diwali leave started on the 18th, and everyone wanted to be home for that. So the only gap was the 12th to the 15th. Four days.
Then I asked, what fixes everything else? Transport. There's one good overnight bus from our city to Hampi on those days, with only a few seats. If we didn't get it, no trip. So we booked the bus first, the same evening. Only after that did we choose a guesthouse, and there were plenty to pick from.
If we'd picked the guesthouse first, we'd have been stuck with rooms and no way to get there.

qa.a: On the 16th.

qa.a: Kiran sounds proud and pleased, calling it a secret and joking about being the calendar nerd.

subtype: Approach: a shared expense sheet and advance deposit [Action]
passage:
Afreen, you're off to Coorg with seven friends? Before you go, let me, your Lalit uncle, tell you about my college trip to Ooty, and the fight that nearly ended a friendship.
We didn't keep track of anything. One person paid the bus, another the hotel, someone bought dinner, someone else the boat ride. On the last night we sat with a torn sheet of paper trying to remember who owed what. Voices rose. My friend Ravi said I was cheating him out of 300. I wasn't, but I couldn't prove it.
On the next trip we did it properly. Before leaving, each of us put 2,000 into one friend's account. Every payment came from there, and he wrote it in a notebook: date, what, how much. At the end, whatever was left was split back. No fights, no torn paper.
Now you have phones. Make a shared sheet. Put the money in one place first.

qa.q: How much did each friend put into one account on the next trip?
How did Lalit feel when Ravi said he was being cheated?
qa.a: Lalit felt hurt and helpless, knowing it wasn't true but unable to prove it.

qa.q: Which choice on the next trip prevented the arguments?
qa.a: Putting money into one account before leaving and writing down every payment, so the record settled things.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt on that last night in Ooty?
qa.a: Ravi was probably frustrated and suspicious, unsure of the numbers, which made him lash out at a friend.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a messy trip without records, then a later trip with an upfront deposit in one account and every payment logged.

On day two, the network vanished for eighteen hours. Pallavi paid the guesthouse in cash, then the taxi to the monastery, then a round of butter tea. Instead of trusting memory, Farhan wrote each one in the back of his diary, with the time.
When the signal returned in a café, he typed all nine entries into the sheet while the others ate. Spent so far: 11,400 of the 18,000.
On the last evening, one friend asked if the taxi had really cost 1,800. Pallavi just opened the sheet, and there it was, with the time next to it. The conversation moved on to photos.

subtype: Approach: leaving planning to the last moment [Pitfall]

Friday, 14 June
It's over before it started. Since March, the six of us have said 'Darjeeling in June, we'll book later'. Every time someone asked about dates, Parul said, 'Relax, we'll figure it out.' And I agreed, because planning felt like homework.
Last week I finally checked. Train: waiting list 140. Flights to Bagdogra: nearly four times what we'd guessed. The homestay we liked: full.
Tonight on the group call we tried to cut it down to two days in Siliguri. Then two people dropped out because it wasn't worth it anymore. Then Parul said maybe next year. Nobody argued.
I feel so flat. It's not even the trip, it's that we had three months and wasted them saying 'later'.
Next time I'm the annoying one who books in March.
– Ayesha

qa.a: Waiting list 140.

qa.a: Ayesha feels flat and disappointed, less about losing the trip than about three months wasted saying 'later'.

passage:
Tuesday night
Trip meeting for Kerala, four days in October. We each wrote two must-dos on chits. Mine: Munnar tea hills and Thekkady. Arnab: an Alleppey houseboat and the Varkala cliffs. Divya: Fort Kochi and Kovalam beach. Sam: a Kathakali show and the Athirappilly falls.
Spread on the floor, the chits looked impossible. Arnab counted the road hours: nearly 25 for all of it. In four days!
So we asked a different question: what's everyone's number one? Munnar, the houseboat, Fort Kochi, Kathakali. Three of those are near Kochi, and Munnar is about four hours away. A loop: Kochi, Munnar, Alleppey, back to Kochi.
We voted. Four hands up, nobody's first choice lost. Varkala and the falls go on the 'next time' list.
I thought someone would sulk. Nobody did, because everyone's top pick survived.
– Chandrika

qa.a: Nearly 25.

At the bus stand tea shop in Mandya, the six friends from the agricultural college voted on the trip in two minutes. Shalini had found a resort in Ooty with a heated pool: 4,500 each for two nights. 'Everyone okay?' she asked. Five hands went up quickly. Harish's went up last.
Harish's father sent him 3,000 a month from the sugarcane money, and most of it went on the hostel mess. He did the maths under the table and felt his stomach sink. But everyone else had said yes, and he didn't want to be the one who spoiled it.
He borrowed from his cousin, told no one, and on the trip said he was 'not a pool person'. While the others swam, he sat in the room scrolling his phone. At dinner they ordered dishes he didn't dare share.
On the bus back, Shalini noticed how quiet he was. He said he was tired.

Tushar groaned. 'You'll make it boring.'
'I'll make it survivable.' Shankar shared his screen. One spare day at the end, so a delay wouldn't mean missing the train home. Guesthouses with free cancellation wherever he could find them. And a short list titled 'If it pours': a café with board games, a gurudwara with a langar, a small museum in Bhuntar.
On day two, a landslide blocked the road to the village they'd planned to hike to. The group spent the afternoon in the board-game café, then used the spare day for the hike once the road opened. Tushar admitted, 'Okay, not boring.'

In the college canteen in Kolkata, Vidya drew three columns on a paper napkin: 'Plan', 'If late', 'If rain'. The group of five was going to Gangtok in September, and Tushar wanted to fill every day.
'Buses and jeeps on that highway can be hours late,' Vidya said. 'If we plan every hour, one delay ruins everything.' Under 'If late' she wrote: one spare day before the train back. Under 'If rain': the monastery museum, a tea tasting, the flower show. And next to each booking: free cancellation, yes or no.
Tushar sighed but moved the monastery trek to day two.
On the way up, their shared jeep was stuck behind a broken-down truck for five hours. They reached Gangtok at midnight instead of seven. Day one was gone, but day four was spare. Nobody had to rebook the train, and the guesthouse, booked with free changes, shifted their first night at no cost.

qa.a: Vidya was cautious and a little worried about a tight plan, and wanted a spare day and backups so she could feel calm about it.

Farida, you asked how our Pondicherry trip didn't turn into a money fight. It's Lakshmi speaking, and honestly, it came down to one conversation.
Before booking, I said to the group, 'Let's be honest about budgets, no shame.' Meena said, a bit quietly, that her allowance is smaller and the sea-view rooms were too much for her. For a second it was awkward. Then Suhana said, 'Fine, so you take the garden-side room. It's cheaper, and it's still the same guesthouse.'
Then we split things into two kinds. Rooms: each pays their own, so Meena pays less. Shared stuff, cabs, the scooter rental, the big dinner: split equally, four ways. We wrote it in the group chat so it was clear.
On the trip, nobody looked at Meena funny at checkout. And later she told me she'd almost not come, before that talk.

qa.a: The garden-side room, which was cheaper.

We'd found a homestay with two kinds of rooms: big ones with a balcony, and a smaller one at the back for less. Aditi asked everyone to fill in a short form: 'What can you spend on the room, honestly? Only I'll see it.' That evening she said, 'Okay, Farzana takes the back room, it suits her. The jeep, the coffee-estate tour and meals, we split equally.'
Farzana went a bit pink, then smiled. Nobody asked why.
At the end, the jeep bill came to 4,800, and Aditi divided it by six: 800 each, the same for everyone. I watched Farzana pay her share without hesitating. I don't know what she felt inside, but she laughed more on that trip than I'd seen all year.

Amma read it twice. 'And this Mohit?'
'He's organising. His number's there. So is the guesthouse owner's.'

Amma had been tight-lipped about the trip for a week. That night she only said, 'Call when you reach.' At 6:40 the next morning, Aparna did.

Elizabeth, your trip money's running low on day two and you want to come home? Wait. Let me, Rashmi, your old hostel senior, tell you about Coorg in my final year.
Six of us. By the second evening we'd spent almost half of what we'd planned for four days: the jeep cost more than we thought, and we'd eaten at the fancy restaurant twice. Someone suggested going home early.
Instead we sat on the homestay steps and made changes. We skipped the river rafting, the most expensive thing left. We bought rice, dal and vegetables and cooked dinner in the homestay kitchen, with the owner's permission; she even lent us her pressure cooker. And for the last day we chose the free viewpoints and a walk through the coffee estates instead of paid tours.
That dinner, all six of us burning the dal, is the best memory of the whole trip.
So, what's the most expensive thing left on your list?

qa.q: Which activity did the group skip?
qa.a: The river rafting.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt on that second evening?
qa.a: Rashmi was probably worried and disappointed, seeing almost half the money gone with two days left.

qa.q: What choice in the story saved the trip?
qa.a: Sitting down to change the plan instead of leaving: skipping rafting, cooking one dinner and choosing free viewpoints.

qa.q: How might the homestay owner have seen the students cooking?
qa.a: The owner seemed kind and glad to help, lending a pressure cooker to a group trying to manage.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a trip where spending ran high by day two, so the group skipped a paid activity, cooked a meal and chose free viewpoints instead of leaving.

subtype: Approach: replanning when money runs short mid-trip [Revision]

On day two in Mcleodganj, Gurleen checked the group's expense sheet and went quiet. They had spent 9,800 of their 16,000 already, and three days were left. The only ATM near their guesthouse had been out of cash since morning.
'We could just go back tomorrow,' Sharmila said.
'Or we fix it,' Gurleen said. 'Let's look at what's left.' The paragliding, 1,500 each for the four of them, was the biggest item. They dropped it. Sharmila found a small shop with vegetables and eggs, and the guesthouse let them use its kitchen for one dinner. For the last day, instead of the paid cable car, they walked to the Bhagsu waterfall and the free viewpoint above Dharamkot.
On the final night Gurleen updated the sheet: 15,100 spent. 900 left over, and all four of them still there.

qa.q: How much had the group spent by day two?
What was Gurleen feeling when the sheet showed 9,800 spent, and what did Gurleen choose to do?
qa.a: Gurleen felt worried and went quiet, but chose to look calmly at what was left instead of giving up.

qa.q: What else could the group do if the ATM stayed empty?
qa.a: Ask the guesthouse owner where else cash is available or which other ways of paying they accept.

qa.q: How does the change of plan feel to Sharmila, who wanted to go back?
qa.a: Sharmila, who first suggested leaving, gets three more days with friends and a waterfall walk instead of an early bus home.

grounding: Shows friends seeing on day two that spending is too high and changing the plan, dropping a paid activity, cooking once and choosing free sights instead of leaving.
